entries.name: The Luciferians
entries.informalName: The Followers of Lucifer of Cagliari
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Good for so small a group. Lucifer's own pamphlets from his exile survive whole. So does a petition that two of his priests sent to the emperors in 383 or 384. Jerome's dialogue against them, Augustine and the Greek church historians give the other side. No text of theirs after the 380s is in hand. A modern editor thinks the group died out early in the 400s. Socrates, writing later, says it still stood apart in his day.
entries.floorNote: No question. They held the creed of Nicaea, and held it more strictly than most.
entries.relationsSummary: They began as the hardest of the Nicene party. Lucifer wrote against the emperor Constantius and the bishops who took his creed. In 362 the church agreed to let bishops who had given way keep their sees. Lucifer's followers would not accept them, and stood apart. Jerome wrote a dialogue against them, and Augustine said they had cut themselves off. In 383 or 384 two of their priests asked the emperors for protection, and the emperors granted it.
entries.why: In 359 almost every bishop of the West signed a creed the emperor wanted. Later most of them took it back. The church then let them keep their places. A small party said no. A bishop who had given way once, they held, could never lead the church again. Their stand shows how hard it was to heal the church after the fights over the creed. It also left the losing side's case in its own words.
entries.teaser: Sardinia, Rome and Antioch, from about 355 — hard-line Nicene Christians. They would not forgive the bishops who had signed the emperor's creed, and they answered to no name but Christian.
entries.longDescription:
Lucifer was bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. At a council in Milan he refused to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, and he stood up to the emperor Constantius II to his face. For this he was sent into exile from 355 to 361. He spent most of those years at Eleutheropolis in Palestine. From there he wrote pamphlets to the emperor himself. How could Christians meet, he asked, with the false bishops of the emperor's sect, the Arians? One pamphlet bears the title We Must Die for the Son of God.

In 362, after Constantius died, the exiles came home. A council met at Alexandria under Athanasius. It agreed that bishops who had only given way could stay in their sees. Lucifer did not attend. Two of his deacons signed its letter for him. He went instead to Antioch and made Paulinus bishop of one of the rival parties there. When his friend Eusebius of Vercelli did not approve, Lucifer broke off communion with him. The church historian Socrates says that many followed Lucifer, and a separate sect arose.

Lucifer himself went home to Sardinia and died there in 371. His followers held on. Hilary, a deacon of Rome, went further than Lucifer. He set up his own font and baptized again those who came over from the Arian side. In about 379 Jerome wrote a dialogue against the group. Lucifer was a good shepherd, he said. But in a time of wolves he took a few sheep away and left the rest of the flock to the beasts.

In Rome the group had its own bishop, Ephesius, and a priest, Macarius, who held night vigils in a private house. In 383 or 384 two of its priests, Marcellinus and Faustinus, sent a petition to the emperors. It says that the clergy of Damasus, bishop of Rome, broke up one of Macarius's vigils and dragged him over the stones. The two priests refused the name Luciferians. Christ is our teacher, they wrote, so the only name we bear is Christian.

The emperors answered them. Their letter called the two men priests full of faith. It told the prefect Cynegius to shield Gregory in Spain, Heraclida in the East and priests like them from attack. The group never grew large. Augustine wrote that they had cut themselves off from the unity of the church. Socrates, writing in the next century, says that those who first joined Lucifer's quarrel still stood apart. After that they fade from view.
voices: Lucifer of Cagliari — bishop in Sardinia, exiled from 355 to 361 for standing by Athanasius, who wrote his pamphlets to the emperor Constantius himself
Hilary the deacon — a deacon of Rome who joined Lucifer's side and baptized again those who came over from the Arians; known through Jerome
Marcellinus — a priest who signed the petition of 383 or 384 to the emperors
Faustinus — a priest who signed the same petition, calling himself unworthy to be called a priest of God
Ephesius — the group's bishop at Rome, whom the petition says Damasus tried to bring before a judge
entries.legacy:
The group did not last, but its case lives on in its own words. Its petition was kept in a Roman book of letters from emperors and popes, the Collectio Avellana. Lucifer's pamphlets survive whole. Jerome's dialogue against the group holds his famous line on the council of Ariminum: the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

The quarrel also raised an older question, which Jerome traces back to Cyprian. Should people baptized outside the church be baptized again when they come in?

entries.name: The Carthusians — The Later Medieval Charterhouses
entries.informalName: The Keepers of the English Books of Prayer
entries.region: Chartreuse, Mount Grace, Sheen, London, Beauvale, Monnikhuizen
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Thin to moderate, and mostly English. The one book in hand by a Carthusian of these years is Nicholas Love's English life of Christ, made before 1410. The rest is the work of the order's hands: names and notes that Carthusian scribes left in the books they copied, as modern editors print them. Thomas à Kempis gives a view from the Low Countries. Nothing in hand comes from the Grande Chartreuse itself in these years. The order's great Latin writers of the age, such as Ludolph of Saxony and Denys the Carthusian, are not yet in hand.
entries.relationsSummary: The same order as the first Carthusians, still keeping its old rule of the cell. In England its monks copied and kept the books of the English mystics, The Cloud of Unknowing and Walter Hilton's Scale of Perfection. Nicholas Love, prior of Mount Grace, attacked the Lollards in his life of Christ. In the Low Countries a Carthusian prior turned Geert Grote's life around, and Grote went on to found the New Devotion.
entries.why: The Carthusians lived alone in their cells, but they read and copied a great deal. In England they became keepers of the new books of prayer written in English. Their scribes copied The Cloud of Unknowing and Hilton's Scale of Perfection, wrote notes in them and passed them on. One of their priors put the life of Christ into plain English for readers who knew no Latin. Modern editors of the Cloud and the Scale still lean on copies made in their houses.
entries.teaser: Charterhouses from Yorkshire to the Low Countries, 1300 to 1534 — silent monks who copied and kept the English books of prayer. One of them put the life of Christ into plain English.
entries.longDescription:
After 1300 the Carthusians kept the life Bruno had begun, each monk alone in his cell under a strict rule. Thomas à Kempis, writing in the Low Countries, thought the light of the heavenly life still shone among them, though hidden. To worldly men their rule seemed harsh, he wrote, but men of fervent spirit chose it gladly. In England the order had houses at Mount Grace in Yorkshire, at Beauvale, at Sheen near the royal palace of Richmond, and in London.

The English houses became keepers of books. Walter Hilton, an Augustinian canon who died in the 1390s, was close to the order. A letter of his is addressed to Adam Horsley, a monk of Beauvale. Carthusian scribes copied his Scale of Perfection with care. In 1499 Grenehalgh, a monk of Sheen, signed a fine copy of it with his own hand. Another copy bears a note that it was a book of the London Charterhouse.

The Cloud of Unknowing went the same way. Richard Methley, a monk of Mount Grace, probably made a Latin version of it. William Tregoose of the London Charterhouse, who died in 1514, wrote out another copy. A note in its margin praises Hilton, whom the notes take to be the author: O most holy Hilton, great is your humility!

Nicholas Love, prior of Mount Grace, wrote an English book that was copied many times. Before 1410 he made The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ out of a Latin life of Christ. He says he wrote it in English for lay men and women of simple understanding. Such readers, he says, need the milk of light teaching. The book is also aimed at the Lollards. Love breaks off to rebuke the Lollard who laughs at the church's miracles of the sacrament. Its editor says it was presented in 1410 to Archbishop Arundel, a hard foe of the Lollards.

Across the sea the order touched another movement. A Carthusian prior of Monnikhuizen, near Arnhem, was an old friend of Geert Grote. He met Grote in Utrecht and urged him to change his life. Grote went to the Carthusians at Monnikhuizen and was given a cell as a guest. Thomas à Kempis tells the story in his life of Grote, the first of the founders of the New Devotion.
voices: Nicholas Love — prior of Mount Grace, who made an English life of Christ before 1410 and attacked the Lollards in it
Richard Methley — a monk of Mount Grace, probably the maker of a Latin version of The Cloud of Unknowing
Grenehalgh — a monk of Sheen who signed a copy of Hilton's Scale of Perfection in 1499 with his own hand
William Tregoose — a monk of the London Charterhouse who wrote out a copy of The Cloud of Unknowing and died in 1514
entries.legacy:
The care of these houses still shapes how the English mystics are read. Evelyn Underhill based her 1923 edition of Hilton's Scale on the London Charterhouse copy. Justin McCann checked his 1924 text of the Cloud against the Latin version made at Mount Grace. Love's Mirror was copied again and again; its 1908 editor knew of twenty-three manuscripts. When the English houses fell under Henry VIII, some of the books are said to have gone with the monks into exile.

The end came in the 1530s, when Henry VIII made himself head of the church in England. In May 1535 John Houghton, prior of the London Charterhouse, was hanged at Tyburn with the priors of Beauvale and Axholme. Many of their brothers followed them to the scaffold or died in Newgate prison, and some escaped to found an English charterhouse at Bruges.

links.note: The Luciferian petition of 383 or 384 says that the clergy of Damasus, bishop of Rome, broke up a night vigil held by the priest Macarius. It says they dragged him over the stones. This rests on the petition alone; no account from Damasus's side is in hand.

links.note: After 362 Lucifer's followers broke with the main church. It had taken back bishops who gave way. Socrates says a new sect arose and still stood apart in his day. The group's own petition rejects the name Luciferians. Augustine says they cut themselves off from the unity of the church.

sources.work: Socrates, Church History 3.9 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: not only separated himself from communion with him, but also began, in a contentious spirit, to condemn what had been determined by the Synod. These things occurring at a season of grievous disorder, alienated many from the church; for many attached themselves to Lucifer, and thus a distinct sect arose under the name of ‘Luciferians.’

sources.work: Socrates, Church History 3.9 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: such as at first identified themselves with his quarrel, still continue separate from the church.

links.note: Augustine warns his readers not to listen to the Luciferians. They do not baptize again, he says, and in that they do right. But they cut themselves off from the unity of the church, and would rather be called Luciferians than Catholics.

links.note: The Carthusian order went on after 1300 under the same rule of the cell. Thomas à Kempis, writing in the 1400s, says the light of the heavenly life still shone among the Carthusians. Nicholas Love, prior of the order's house at Mount Grace, wrote before 1410.

links.note: Carthusian monks copied and kept the books of the English mystics. In 1499 Grenehalgh, a monk of Sheen, signed a copy of Walter Hilton's Scale of Perfection. William Tregoose of the London Charterhouse, who died in 1514, wrote out The Cloud of Unknowing and praised Hilton in its margin.

links.note: Thomas à Kempis tells how the Carthusian prior of Monnikhuizen, an old friend, urged Geert Grote to change his life. Grote then went to the Carthusians at Monnikhuizen, near Arnhem, and they gave him a cell as a guest.
